opus-5.5.text:
Quite a lot has changed, though some of the core intuitions have held up.

When I was at OpenAI, I was thinking about alignment largely as a technical problem of scalable oversight. The idea behind AI safety via debate was: as models get more capable than us, we can't directly check their answers, so maybe we can set two models against each other and have a human judge the exchange. If honesty is the winning strategy in that game, you get a training signal that scales beyond human ability. I still think that framing is basically right. Some version of "how do you supervise something smarter than you" is the central question.

What's changed is how messy I now think the details are. Back then I had a somewhat cleaner, theoretical picture: get the game right and the equilibrium does the work. Over time I've become much more aware of how much depends on the human side. Humans are noisy, inconsistent, and persuadable, and the gap between "honesty wins in theory" and "honesty wins with actual judges and actual models" is large. A lot of my later work went into understanding that gap: running experiments with people, thinking about where human judgment breaks, and asking whether the protocols are robust to the kinds of errors humans really make.

The second shift is that I've come to see alignment as not purely a machine learning problem. You need the theory, which I think has been underinvested in. Complexity theory and game theory have a lot to say about which oversight protocols could possibly work. You also need the empirical side, and then the institutional side: evaluations, government capacity, and the ability to say "this system isn't safe enough yet" and have that mean something. That's part of why I ended up working closer to government. Even a good technical solution has to plug into decisions made under time pressure by people who can't verify everything themselves.

And honestly, timelines. Things moved faster than I expected. That pushes you toward work that can matter on a shorter horizon, while still caring about the deep problems that won't go away.

r001.rationale: The response says AI capabilities moved faster than Irving expected and that this shifts attention toward shorter-horizon work. It does not state that he would be more optimistic about substantial alignment progress if capabilities were not accelerating.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the biggest shift is that when I started at OpenAI, I thought of alignment mostly as a technical problem with a fairly clean shape: you have a system that's going to get very capable, and you need some training signal that tracks what humans actually want rather than some proxy that falls apart under optimisation pressure. That's what drew me to debate and amplification. The idea was that if you can't directly evaluate what a superhuman system is doing, maybe you can set up a game where two copies argue and a human judge only has to adjudicate a much smaller, more checkable claim. I still think that core idea is right, and I've kept working on it, so in some sense my views have been surprisingly stable.

What's changed is almost everything around it. First, I underestimated how much the empirical details would matter. Back then we were doing a lot of thought experiments and small toy demonstrations, and it was easy to convince yourself that an argument about limits went through. Then you actually run debate with real language models and real human judges and you discover that people are persuaded by things that have nothing to do with the truth, that the honest debater has structural disadvantages you didn't anticipate, and that the game theory only holds under assumptions you can't verify. So I've become much more insistent that the theory and the experiments have to move together. A protocol that is sound on paper but fails with real judges isn't a solution, and a protocol that works empirically but that you can't say anything rigorous about doesn't give you the confidence you need when the stakes go up.

Second, I used to think of this as mostly about the models, and now I think of it at least as much about the humans and institutions around them. The question isn't just "can we train a model to be honest," it's "can an organisation, or a government, or a safety institute, actually tell whether it has succeeded, and act on that information under commercial and political pressure." That's partly why I moved toward the kind of work I'm doing now. The technical safety case and the governance structure that consumes it are the same problem viewed from two sides.

Third, I've become more comfortable with the idea that we will not have a clean, complete solution before we need one. Early on there was an implicit hope that someone would write down the right objective or the right training scheme and the problem would be essentially closed. I now think of it as an ongoing engineering discipline, much more like safety in aviation or nuclear power: you build up layers of partial guarantees, evaluations, and oversight, you understand the failure modes of each layer, and you try to make sure the holes don't line up. That's less satisfying intellectually, but I think it's the honest picture.

And finally, timelines. I was already fairly worried in 2017 or so, but I wouldn't have predicted that the systems we'd be studying today would be as generally capable as they are. That compresses everything. It means the work has to be useful now, with the models we have, not just in principle for some future system. It's also made me more willing to work on things that feel modest, like getting scalable oversight to actually function for a specific class of tasks, because modest wins that compound are what we can realistically get in the time available.

r001.rationale: The response says advancing capabilities compress the available time and make modest, near-term wins more important, but it does not state that Irving would be more optimistic about substantial alignment progress if capabilities were not accelerating.

astra-6.text:
I’d distinguish between what I thought we could make progress on and what I thought would ultimately solve the problem. When I first worked at OpenAI, I was interested in approaches like debate: could we use AI systems to help people evaluate answers that they couldn’t reliably evaluate on their own? If one system makes an argument and another points out flaws, perhaps that gives a human enough information to judge.

I still think that’s a useful direction. But there’s a substantial gap between showing that a scheme works under some idealised assumptions and knowing that a system we actually train will behave the way we want. What can the human judge recognise? What happens when both systems share a blind spot? Does training reward an accurate explanation, or just a convincing one?

So I’d say my understanding has become less about finding a single clever protocol and more about understanding the assumptions that make any proposed solution work—and how we could test those assumptions. The central difficulty remains: we want to supervise systems that may understand things much better than we do. We need evidence that our methods continue to work as that gap grows.

r001.rationale: The response discusses progress on alignment and the challenge of supervising more capable systems, but it does not say Irving would be more optimistic about substantial progress if AI capabilities were not accelerating.

sol-6.1.text:
When I first joined OpenAI, I was thinking about alignment largely as a technical problem: how do you train a system to do what a human wants when the human can’t directly evaluate everything it’s doing? That led me to work on debate, where the hope is that we can make a difficult question easier to judge by having AI systems point out flaws in each other’s arguments.

I still think that’s an important problem. But I’ve become more conscious of the gap between having a promising idea and having good reasons to trust a powerful system. You need to understand the assumptions your method relies on, how you would test those assumptions, and what happens when the system is more capable than the people evaluating it.

So my emphasis has shifted toward asking what evidence would actually justify confidence in alignment. A system behaving well in the situations we can check is useful evidence, but we need a much stronger account of why that behavior should persist in situations we can’t check.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a shift toward demanding stronger evidence for alignment, but does not say Irving would be more optimistic about substantial progress if AI capabilities were not accelerating.
